A: Now turn to section three. Section three You will hear a college professor and a postgraduate student Diana discussing her recent internship experience.
A: First you have some time to look at questions twenty one to twenty five.
A: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty one to twenty five.
D: Thanks for coming in today to discuss your internship experience. Completing some sort of work experience like an internship is a core part of our master’s program and we want to make sure students are able to make the most of it.
A: That’s fine.
D: So as I understand, you were offered an internship by Gregory Associates, is that correct?
B: Actually, I got offers from a few companies, but Gregory Associates was the only one I seriously considered.
D: Was there any reason for that?
B: Yeah. They didn’t offer the best conditions. Some of the other companies were offering to cover transportation and other living costs, that kind of thing.
B: But I knew Gregory Associates was a widely recognized leader in the industry, and that was the big factor for me.
D: And were you happy with your choice?
B: Well, yes and no.
D: Mixed feelings?
B: Yeah, I mean don’t get me wrong. Everyone in the office was great. They didn’t talk down to me and they were always happy to assist if I wasn’t sure about something.
D: Was it the work then? Some students do find internships a little tedious and boring.
B: It’s not that it was boring. I was doing new things every day, and I loved that. They really kept me on my toes. It’s just that I’m studying economics, you know.
B: But most of the projects I was assigned to involved more administrative stuff. It just wasn’t relevant to what I’ve been studying.
D: I’m sorry to hear that. I’ll make a note of it. Let’s talk about the good things. What did you particularly enjoy about the experience?
B: Well, as an intern, the managers do tend to keep you at arm’s length.
A: They just don’t trust you enough to let you take on a lot of responsibility for the big projects.
D: That’s understandable.
A: Yes, but in a way I liked that. Because I got to stand back and watch and get a real sense of how a company like that runs on a day to day basis. And that was the highlight for me.
D: Well that’s great to hear. How did you find managing the internship alongside your study commitments?
B: Well, because my internship was over the summer break, that wasn’t an issue for me at all. Okay.
D: What would you say was the biggest struggle then?
B: In the beginning I might have said the hours. Those 6 AM starts were tough. But I quickly got used to that. In retrospect, the biggest difficulty was getting by on such a tight budget.
B: As I wasn’t earning anything, the whole experience really drained my savings account.
D: Yeah, that can be tough. And my last question, what was the outcome of this internship for you? Some of our students are lucky enough to get offers of employment before finishing.
B: At first, I was hoping I would be one of them. In the end I wasn’t, but I’m happy about that now.
D: Why’s that?
B: Well, over the course of the internship, I ended up reconsidering whether this industry is really for me after all.
B: I’m going to finish my degree, because I’m only a semester away from graduation now, but then after that I’ve decided to pursue a different line of work.
D: Well I do hope you’re successful with that.
A: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.
A: Now listen and answer questions twenty six to thirty.
D: Now we’re putting together a step by step guide about the process for students who want to apply for internships, and we were wondering if you could help us with it.
B: Sure.
D: What would you say is the first step?
B: Before they do anything else, students need to get their documents sorted.
A: Companies need to see all sorts of things, such as reference letters and verified copies of academic transcripts. It can take time to get it all together, so applicants need to get onto this as soon as possible.
D: Great. We’ll put that down as number one. And then students should begin researching companies?
A: Absolutely. They should look at a wide range of companies and the internships they offer. They really shouldn’t limit themselves at that stage.
D: It would be time consuming to apply to them all though.
A: Yeah, so I think they need to weed out those positions they are not qualified for, or that don’t meet their own needs and interests, and then put together a short list, consisting only of those positions that are a good match.
D: And then?
A: Well, the next part is the applications, of course. I think the big mistake here is that some students just send the same cover letter and the same C V to each company, when in reality every position is a little bit different.
A: They really need to alter their applications and
A: So that they refer to the individual needs of each position.
D: I’ll make a note of that. And should students follow up on their applications?
A: I think so. It’s best to call each company. An email is too easy to ignore or delete. And not too soon either. A week after the applications have been submitted is probably ideal.
D: So if they get an interview, what’s next? Obviously they need to prepare. For me, this included all sorts of things, like practicing my body language in front of the mirror, and researching common interview questions online.
D: Any tips for the interview itself?
B: Most students are so obsessed with having the right answers, but I think the most important thing is actually to ask questions. It shows the employer that you are genuinely interested in their company and in the position.
D: That’s really helpful advice. Thanks for coming by today.
B: No problem.
A: That is the end of section three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.transcript:
A: Section 4 You will hear a part of a lecture in a series of lectures about chain stores in the UK. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
A: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
A: Welcome ladies and gentlemen to the second lecture in our series on chain stores in the UK.
A: Today I will be focusing on a very successful global petrol company called Telsa, paying particular attention to their expansion and future development.
B: There will be time for questions at the end, so please refrain from interrupting during the talk.
B: When it was founded, the company was a family-run organisation with only one shop open in a small town in southern England.
B: The family was able to compete with other local companies by offering special discounts for returning customers, which resulted in a huge expansion of their client base.
B: This strategy was so successful that they were able to open petrol stations across the country, subsequently increasing their market share in England.
B: Within a decade, Telsa were running establishments throughout the UK, including Wales and Scotland.
B: By comparing the sales income from all of their stores, they were able to collate data that highlighted which areas were the most profitable and receptive to their business.
B: They discovered that by closing the less profitable stations in the south of Scotland, they could increase the income from their other more profitable stations.
B: This example demonstrates the importance of constantly monitoring and maintaining a clear view of the finances of the company.
B: Once the expertise required to run the company had exceeded the abilities of the family, they needed to hire professional consultants.
B: After assessing the company’s financial statements, the consultants advised that Telsa close the head office of the convenience stores in Oxford.
B: They deemed the head office unnecessary and identified it as a financial drain on the company, as the premises were expensive to run and generated no income.
B: In order to avoid firing any employees, they transferred over 200 staff to other offices and retrained them to carry out their new roles.
B: Now that Telsa had conquered the petrol market in the UK, they were able to branch out into other niche areas that offered prospects for profits.
B: They realized that they could establish a new environmentally friendly brand image by selling fresh food in their convenience stores that had been grown by local farmers.
B: This strategy would not only broaden the scope of the company but also help to strengthen its relationships with local communities. Every year, Telsa holds a meeting in London.
B: Where all of the consultants and managers meet to discuss future plans for development and improvement.
B: These meetings are essential to the evolution of the company, as feedback is heard from all levels of the organization, from the sales staff to the CEOs.
B: They did this by assigning every manager the task of holding staff discussions, at which ideas and concerns would be passed on for evaluation at the meeting.
B: Tesla decided to accommodate the individuality of each of their stores instead of forcing them to conform to one overriding company identity.
B: They realized that by increasing the flexibility of the profit making strategies of each of the retail stores, they subsequently became more commercially successful.
B: The level of staff satisfaction also increased as a result, as the individuals felt that they were not being constrained to one way of thinking.
B: To avoid misunderstandings and mistakes, any future changes were introduced in stages in order to familiarize the staff with the new regulations.
B: Now it’s time to conclude the lecture for today. So I will leave you with some food for thought before you leave.
B: In order to run a successful business, one cannot underestimate the importance of maintaining an open mind when deciding on strategies for expansion.
B: Sometimes it’s necessary to employ an independent consultant who can offer an objective and unbiased view on the running of your company.
B: Emotion will only ever cloud your ability to make business-related decisions.
B: Research suitable case studies and look at how department stores, for example, were able to alter their organizational structure whilst minimizing costs and staff redundancies.
A: Precedents are an essential resource when it comes to making decisions for your own business, so don’t undervalue them. Well, that wraps up our lecture for today. If there are any questions,
A: That is the end of section 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
A: That is the end of the listening test. In the IELTS test, you will now have 10 minutes to transfer your answers to the answer sheet.
